title: Get to know change
hook: study how all things change into one another (Meditations 10.11)

segments.voice: Yesterday: keep the names. Your line was keep the name. Which name did you live, and did you come back when you slipped? Day six hundred sixteen, the end of a week.

Take one photo of the same tree every week for a year, and the strip of pictures will astonish you. Buds, leaves, gold, bare branches, snow. It never stops changing; we just don't look closely enough to see it happen. Marcus thought watching change closely was one of the most useful things a person could practice. In book ten he treats it as a whole discipline of its own. Today: get to know change.
screen: `ONE TREE, EVERY WEEK.` → `IT NEVER STOPS.` → `GET TO KNOW CHANGE.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. Learn the way of looking that sees how all things change into one another, Marcus writes. Keep attending to it, and train yourself in this part of philosophy. Second, the reason. Nothing, he says, is so fitted to produce greatness of mind. Someone who really sees that everything is changing loosens their grip. They stop clutching, because there's nothing to clutch that will hold still. Third, what it frees. That person, he says, has in a way already set the body aside, knowing they'll soon leave the human world. They give themselves wholly to justice in what they do, and to the nature of the whole in everything else. What others say or think or do against them doesn't occupy them. Two things are enough for them: to act justly now, and to be content with what is given now. Fourth, the week, looking back. Correct or be kind. The smallest thing. Let me not fear. Simple and whole. Made to bear it. Keep the name. And now, study change. Under all seven lies the same ground: things are moving. People change, troubles end, prayers turn, names slip and come back. Watch change closely, and you hold everything a little more lightly, and act a little more justly. Marcus calls that greatness of mind, and he thinks you build it by looking.
screen: `SEE HOW ALL THINGS CHANGE.` · `IT BUILDS GREATNESS OF MIND.` · `JUSTICE NOW, CONTENT NOW.` · `A WEEK OF THINGS MOVING.` · then, large: `STUDY CHANGE.`

segments.voice: If you can, look at something that is changing right now: a cloud, a candle flame, a cup of tea cooling, light moving across a wall, your own breath. Watch it the whole time. Don't think about it. Just see it change, second by second. When your mind wanders, come back to the change. Notice how much is happening in what looked still. The bell holds the time.
Get to know change. Marcus's discipline: watch how all things turn into one another. Nothing, he says, builds greatness of mind like it. Today's word.
Your line: study change. Pick one thing today, a tree, a face, the sky, and look at how it has changed since the last time you really looked. Day six hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Stoic readers often practice contemplating change, watching a flame, a season or their own body, as a way to hold things more lightly and to stay focused on acting justly now.

original.note: Greek: change, a turning into something else; the root of the English metabolism.

trapdoor: what you thought: everything changes, so whatever.
what it means: train your eyes to see change, and you'll hold things lightly and act justly now.
what a scholar hears: the English word metabolism comes from the same Greek family as metabolē, change.
